Name: Adam
Transcript: Good to see you again. Last time was March, before the season started. So, to begin, what's the plot like for you now, at midsummer?

Name: Hollis
Transcript: Oh, it's a different place. I go every day now. Every single day. Even when it rains I go down and stand in the shed and watch it rain. I've put a door on the shed, and a chair in it, a proper one, Pat's old kitchen chair. I'm down there by seven most mornings, and some days I'm not back till the news is on. Pat says I've moved out. And in a way I have. The flat's where I sleep now, and the plot's where I live. That's how it feels. I wake up and the first thing I think is, I wonder if the onions are all right. Not, what am I going to do with myself. That's gone, that feeling. I don't miss it.

Name: Adam
Transcript: Pat says you've moved out. How does she say it?

Name: Hollis
Transcript: Mostly as a joke. Mostly. There was one night in June, I came in at nine, filthy, and my tea was in the oven gone hard, and she said, I didn't marry you for your runner beans. And we had words. Not a row. Words. She said, a year ago you were under my feet and now I never see you, you can't win with you. And I thought, she's right, you can't win with me. I'd gone from one end to the other. So I've been trying. I bring her things back. Sweet peas. She likes a sweet pea. She put them in a jug on the windowsill and she didn't say anything, but she put them where she could see them from her chair. That went down all right, I think.

Name: Adam
Transcript: You'd gone from one end to the other. What was that like to see?

Name: Hollis
Transcript: Not very nice, if I'm honest. I'd been that pleased with myself, out from under her feet, I never thought she might miss me. Daft, after forty-odd years. I thought she wanted the flat back. And she did. But she didn't want it empty either. She said, I got used to you, and now you've gone again. Like the depot all over. And that went in, that did. Forty-one years she had the flat to herself all day, and then she had a year of me, and then she had nobody again. So now I come home at one for my dinner. We have our dinner together, the two of us, and then I go back down. It's like a shift, the day. Two halves with dinner in the middle.

Name: Adam
Transcript: Last time you talked about the old boys at the gate. How are things there?

Name: Hollis
Transcript: Better. Much better. One of them, Frank, came over in May, stood at the end of my plot with his hands behind his back like a foreman, and told me my onions were too close together. Just that. Your onions are too close together, they'll come to nothing. And walked off. I took it as an insult for a whole day. I went home stewing. And then I realised, lying in bed, it was the first thing he'd said to me that wasn't good morning. Two months, and that was the first thing. That's how they say hello down there. They tell you what you've done wrong.

Name: Adam
Transcript: Taking it as an insult for a day. What was that day like?

Name: Hollis
Transcript: I was mad as a wasp. I told Pat. I said, who does he think he is, thirty years on a plot doesn't make you the king of the onions. And she laughed at me. She said, well, they've noticed you, then. And she was right. Same as at the depot. Nobody bothers putting a man right if they don't think he'll be there next month. You don't waste your breath on him. So the next morning I went down and I thinned the onions out, where he could see me doing it. And he walked past and he said, that's better. That's all. That's better. I could have shaken his hand. I didn't, mind. You don't.

Name: Adam
Transcript: You could have shaken his hand.

Name: Hollis
Transcript: I could. I was that pleased. Two months of good morning, and then that's better. It's daft what you'll be pleased about at sixty-eight. At the depot I got a long service award, a plaque with my name on, the manager shook my hand in front of everybody in the canteen. And I'll tell you, that's better from Frank did more for me than the plaque. The plaque's in the cupboard with the Christmas lights. I think about that's better most days.

Name: Adam
Transcript: And the work itself, how has it gone?

Name: Hollis
Transcript: Up and down. The potatoes are coming on lovely. But the beans failed. Every one. Runner beans, the ones Pat was on about. They came up and then something got them, the slugs or the cold nights, I don't know, they just went black and that was that. And I was embarrassed. Properly embarrassed. I put a bit of netting over them so nobody would see. Draped it over like a sheet over a body. Then Maureen, two plots down, she came over and she lifted the netting up and had a look, and she said, mine have gone the same, love. And we stood there laughing at our beans like a pair of fools.

Name: Adam
Transcript: You put netting over them. What was that like?

Name: Hollis
Transcript: Daft, isn't it. Netting over dead beans. But I've always been like that. At the depot you didn't let a bad job be seen. If you'd made a mess of something you sorted it before the foreman came round, and nobody was any the wiser. That's how I was brought up in the trade. But you can't fix a bean. It's dead, it's dead. And when Maureen laughed, it went out of me, the embarrassment. Like letting the air out of a tyre. Everybody's beans had gone. It wasn't me. It was the year. I'd been carrying it like it was me, and it was just the year.

Name: Adam
Transcript: Tell me about Maureen.

Name: Hollis
Transcript: Maureen. Oh, you'll have heard of her if you've been down there. She's been on her plot twenty years. Widow, seventy-four, and she'll talk to anybody. She's the opposite of the old boys. She came over my second week and told me her life story, her husband, her hip, her grandson in the navy. I didn't know what to do with it, to be honest. I'm not used to that, somebody just coming over and talking at you on a site. At the depot nobody did that. But she's the one who told me when the committee meetings are, and where to get muck for nothing, and which tap you don't drink from. Everything I know, near enough, Maureen told me. I never asked her one thing. She just told me.

Name: Adam
Transcript: You said the potatoes are coming on. What's that been like?

Name: Hollis
Transcript: Oh, that's been the best bit. I lifted the first earlies last week, just one root, to see. You put the fork in a bit wide, so you don't spear them, and lift, and there they are. Six, seven potatoes on one plant, white, clean, the size of eggs. I stood there with them in my hand like I'd found money in the street. My own potatoes. Out of ground I'd dug, that was brambles in March. I took them home in my cap. Pat boiled them with a bit of mint and we had them with butter, nothing else, and I'm not ashamed to say it was the best thing I've eaten in years. She said they were very nice. Very nice. I'll take very nice.

Name: Adam
Transcript: How's your body with it now, compared to March?

Name: Hollis
Transcript: Better. A lot better. I've had my belt in two notches. The knees still complain going up the stairs at the flats when the lift's out, which is most weeks, but I can do three hours down there now and walk home. And I sleep. I sleep like I did when I was working, straight through. In March I was frightened of it, the body, I told you that. I'm not frightened of it now. I know what it'll do. I know where it stops.

Name: Adam
Transcript: You know where it stops.

Name: Hollis
Transcript: I've learned to stop before it stops me. That's the trick. I sit on the bucket every hour, on the dot. Cup of tea, five minutes, back up. And here's the funny thing. In March I was ashamed of that. Sitting down. I felt like I was skiving, like somebody was going to come round the corner and catch me. Now I think of it as part of the job. You service an engine, don't you, you don't run it till it seizes. Well I'm the engine. I'm learning that. Sixty-eight years old and I'm learning that.

Name: Adam
Transcript: What's a day like now, down there?

Name: Hollis
Transcript: It's got a shape. That's the thing. I'm down at seven. I do whatever needs doing first, watering if it's dry, before the sun gets on it. Tea on the bucket at nine. Frank comes past about ten and says something about my onions, there's always something. Home at one for dinner with Pat. Back down at three, do the evening jobs, the hoeing, and back up for the news. That's a day. You could set your watch by it. Last year a day was just a lump. Get up, get through it, go to bed. You'd look at the clock at eleven and think, how is it only eleven. Now I look at the clock and think, is it three already.

Name: Adam
Transcript: What's it like when you're on your own there now?

Name: Hollis
Transcript: Still quiet, but a different quiet. In March it was a quiet like an empty room. Now I know the robin, he's still about, he's got a mate now. I know which tap drips, the one by the water butts, I've told the committee twice. I know where the sun comes over the railway at a quarter past seven. It's like the place knows I'm there. That sounds soft. But it's like that. I'm not a visitor there now.

Name: Adam
Transcript: Not a visitor. Tell me more about that.

Name: Hollis
Transcript: Well, in March I'd walk up the path and it was somebody else's place and I was being let in. Now if I miss a day, I feel I've missed something. Somebody's courgettes have come on, or the fox has been at Ken's bins, or there's been a to-do at the committee meeting about the water. And if I'm not there I hear it second-hand. And I don't like hearing it second-hand. I want to have seen it. That's how you know it's yours, I suppose, when you mind missing it.

Name: Adam
Transcript: When you mind missing it. What's that like?

Name: Hollis
Transcript: It's a good feeling, mostly. I'd forgotten it. At the depot you'd come back off your holidays and the first thing you'd want to know was what you'd missed. Who'd done what, which bus was off the road. You minded missing it because you were part of it. Retiring, you don't miss anything. There's nothing to miss. Nothing's going on that you're part of. So when I came down one Monday and Ken said, you missed a right do on Saturday, the fox got in Maureen's hen run, I was proper put out. I was put out I'd missed a fox. That's how I knew.

Name: Adam
Transcript: And the flat, these days?

Name: Hollis
Transcript: The flat's all right in summer. Window open, you can hear the trains and the swifts going round the block screaming. I don't think about the flat much, if I'm honest. I sleep there. Pat's there. That's about it. If I'm really honest, I don't know what I'll do in November. When it's dark at half four and there's nothing to do down there. I've not let myself think about it.

Name: Adam
Transcript: What happens when you start to think about it?

Name: Hollis
Transcript: Same feeling as March. Before March. The part left over. It comes up in my chest a bit, and I push it back down. I tell myself it's July. There's beans to do again, I've put a second lot in, and the potatoes to lift, and I'll worry about November in November. That's what I tell myself. Whether it'll work, I don't know. But it's July.

Name: Adam
Transcript: Is there anything about the plot now that I haven't asked you about?

Name: Hollis
Transcript: The gate. You asked me in March and I said I'd like them to carry on talking. Well, they don't quite. When I come in now, Frank looks up and says, here he is. Here he is. And then they carry on. So it's not quite carrying on, there's the here he is first. But it's near enough. It's near enough for me. I'll take here he is.
